question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
If we let $u = 5x,$ then \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x=\dfrac 15\textrm d u. \]

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

$x$ $0$ $\pi/10$
$u$ $0$ $\pi/2$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \begin{align} \int_{0}^{\pi/10} 4\cos \left(5x\right) \, \textrm{d}x &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2}4\cos{u}\cdot \dfrac 15 \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= \dfrac 4 5 \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \cos{u}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= \dfrac 4 5 \sin u\Big|_{0}^{\pi/2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 4 5\left( \sin \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - \sin(0)\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac 4 5\left(1 - 0\right)\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{4}{5}} \end{align}

question.explanation:
If we let $u = 2x,$ then \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x=\dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u. \]

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ \int \cos(2x) \, \textrm{d}x & =\int \cos u\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] & =\dfrac{1}{2}\int \cos u\,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] & = \dfrac 1 2 \sin u + C \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\sin (2x)}{2} + C } \end{eqnarray}

example.title: Integrating Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments

question.explanation:
If we let $u = 3x,$ then \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x=\dfrac 13\textrm d u. \]

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

$x$ $0$ $\pi/3$
$u$ $0$ $\pi$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \begin{align} \int _{0}^{\pi/3} 2\cos {\left(3x\right)}\, \textrm{d}x &= \int_{0}^{\pi} 2\cos {u}\cdot \dfrac 13\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3}\int_{0}^{\pi} \cos {u}\,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3}\sin {u}\Big|_{0}^{\pi}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3}(\sin{\left(\pi\right)}-\sin 0)\\[5pt] &=0 \end{align}

question.explanation:
If we let $u =5z,$ then

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d z} = 5 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d z =\dfrac 1 5\, \textrm d u. \]

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

\begin{align*} \int \sin(5z) \, \textrm{d}z &=\int \sin{u}\cdot \dfrac{1}{5}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac 1 5 \int \sin{u}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] & = -\dfrac 1 5 \cos u+ C \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac 1 5 \cos (5z) + C \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
If we let $u= \dfrac{2\pi x}{3},$ then \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x=\dfrac{3}{2\pi} \textrm d u. \]

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

$x$ $0$ $1/2$
$u$ $0$ $\pi/3$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

\begin{align} \int_{0}^{1/2}6\cos{\left(\dfrac{2\pi x}{3}\right)}\, \textrm{d}x &= \int_{0}^{\pi/3} 6\cos {u}\cdot\dfrac{3}{2\pi}\,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{9}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi/3} \cos {u}\,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{9}{\pi}\sin{u}\Big|_{0}^{\pi/3}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{9}{\pi}\left(\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) -\sin\left(0\right)\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{9}{\pi}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} -0\right)\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{2\pi}} \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Integrating Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments

question.explanation:
If we let $u = 2x,$ then \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = \dfrac 12\textrm d u. \]

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

$x$ $\pi/6$ $\pi/4$
$u$ $\pi/3$ $\pi/2$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \begin{align} \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/4} \csc\left(2x \right)\cot\left(2x \right)\, \textrm{d}x &= \int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}\csc {u} \cot {u} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} \csc{u}\cot{u}\,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\csc{u}\Big|_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\csc{\left( \dfrac{\pi}2\right)}- \csc{\left( \dfrac{\pi}3\right)}\right)\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\left(1-\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
If we let $u = 3x,$ then \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{3} \,\textrm{d}u. \]

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

$x$ $\pi/18$ $\pi/9$
$u$ $\pi/6$ $\pi/3$

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \begin{align*} \int_{\pi/18}^{\pi/9} 3\sec^{2}(3x) \,\textrm{d}x &= \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} 3\sec^{2}(u) \cdot \dfrac{1}{3} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \sec^{2}(u) \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \tan(u) \, \Big|_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \\[5pt] &= \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) - \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{3} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}} \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
If we let $u = 3x,$ then \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = \dfrac 13\textrm d u. \]

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

$x$ $\pi/12$ $\pi/9$
$u$ $\pi/4$ $\pi/3$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \begin{align} \int_{\pi/12}^{\pi/9} 6\sec\left(3x \right)\tan\left(3x \right)\, \textrm{d}x &= \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3}6\sec {(u)} \tan {(u)} \cdot \dfrac{1}{3}\,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= 2\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3} \sec{(u)}\tan{(u)}\,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= 2\sec{(u)}\Big|_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3}\\[5pt] &= 2\left(\sec{\left( \dfrac{\pi}3\right)}- \sec{\left( \dfrac{\pi}4\right)}\right)\\[5pt] &= 2\left(2-\sqrt{2}\right)\\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{4-2\sqrt{2}} \end{align}

example.title: Integrating Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments

question.explanation:
If we let $u = \dfrac{x}{3},$ then \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{3}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = 3\, \textrm d u. \]

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

$x$ $0$ $\pi$
$u$ $0$ $\pi/3$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \[ \eqalign{ \int_{0}^{\pi} \dfrac 1 2 \sec {\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)}\tan {\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)} \, \textrm{d}x &= \int_{0}^{\pi/3} \dfrac 12 \sec {u}\tan {u} \cdot 3\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= \dfrac 32 \int_{0}^{\pi/3} \sec {u}\tan {u} \, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac 32 \sec u\Big|_{0}^{\pi/3}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac 32 \left(\sec\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-\sec(0)\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac 32 (2-1)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac 32 } \]

question.explanation:
If we let $u = \tan {x},$ then

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \sec^2 {x}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sec^2 {x}\, \textrm{d}x =\textrm{d}u. \]

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

\begin{align} \int \tan {x} \sec^2 {x} \,\textrm{d}x &= \int u\,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{u^2}{2} + C\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\tan^2{x}}{2} + C \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Integrating Products Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution

question.explanation:
Let $u=x^3.$ Differentiating, we have \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=3x^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d u =3 x^2 \, \textrm d x. \]

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \[ \eqalign{ \int 3x^2\csc\left(x^3 \right)\cot\left(x^3 \right)\, \textrm{d}x &=\int \csc\left(x^3 \right)\cot\left(x^3 \right)\cdot 3x^2 \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\int \csc u\cot u\,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=-\csc u+C\\[5pt] &=-\csc \left(x^3 \right)+C } \]

example.title: Integrating Products Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution

question.explanation:
Let $u=x^3. $ Differentiating, we have \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=3x^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 13\textrm d u = x^2\, \textrm d x. \]

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \[ \eqalign{ \int 5x^2\cos\left(x^3 \right)\, \textrm{d}x &=\int 5\cos\left(x^3 \right)\cdot x^2\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\int 5\cos u \cdot \dfrac{1}{3}\,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{5}{3}\int \cos u\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{5}{3}\sin u+C\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{5}{3}\sin \left(x^3 \right)+C } \]

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
If we let $u = 4x^{2},$ then \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 8x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}u = 8x \, \textrm{d}x. \]

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

$x$ $0$ $\sqrt {\pi/4}$
$u$ $0$ $\pi$

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \begin{align*} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi/4}} 8x\cos\left(4x^{2}\right) \,\textrm{d}x &= \int_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi/4}} \cos\left(4x^{2}\right) \cdot 8x \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi} \cos{(u)} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \sin{(u)} \, \Big|_{0}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \sin(\pi) - \sin(0) \\[5pt] &= 0 - 0 \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0} \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Let $u=x^3$, Differentiating, we have \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=3x^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 13\textrm d u = x^2 \, \textrm d x. \]

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \[ \eqalign{ \int x^2\sec\left(x^3 \right)\tan\left(x^3 \right)\, \textrm{d}x &=\int \sec\left(x^3 \right)\tan\left(x^3 \right)\cdot x^2\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\int \sec u \tan u \cdot \dfrac{1}{3}\,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3}\int \sec u\tan u\,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3}\sec u+C\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3}\sec \left(x^3 \right)+C } \]

question.explanation:
Let $u=x^2.$ Differentiating, we have \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=2x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 12\textrm d u = x \, \textrm d x. \]

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \[ \eqalign{ \int x\sin\left(x^2 \right)\, \textrm{d}x &=\int \sin\left(x^2 \right)\cdot x \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\int \sin u\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int \sin u\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos u+C\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos \left(x^2 \right)+C } \]

exampleAnswers.title: Integrating Quotients Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
If we let $u=2+3\tan (x),$ then \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 3\sec^2 (x) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac13\textrm d u = \sec^2( x) \,\textrm d x. \]

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

$x$ $0$ $\pi/4$
$u$ $2$ $5$

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \begin{align*} \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\sec^2 (x)}{2+3\tan (x)}\,{\textrm{d}x} &= \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{1}{2+3\tan (x)}\cdot \sec^2 (x) \, {\textrm{d}x}\\[5pt] &= \int_{2}^{5} \dfrac{1}{u}\cdot\dfrac13\,{\textrm{d}u}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac13\int_{2}^{5} \dfrac{1}{u}\, {\textrm{d}u}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac13\Big.\ln|u| \Big|_{2}^{5}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac13\left(\ln 5-\ln 2\right)\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac13\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)} \end{align*}

example.title: Integrating Quotients Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution

question.explanation:
Let $u=\csc{x}+2.$ Differentiating, we have \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -\csc{x}\cot{x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\textrm{d}u = \csc{x}\cot{x} \,\textrm{d}x. \]

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \[ \eqalign{ \int \dfrac{2\csc {x}\cot{x}}{\csc{x}+2}\, \textrm{d}x &= 2\int \dfrac{1}{\csc{x}+2}\cdot\csc {x}\cot{x}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= 2\int \dfrac{1}{u}\cdot\left(-\textrm d u\right) \\[5pt] &= -2\int\dfrac{1}{u}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= -2\ln|u|+C\\[5pt] &= -2\ln|\csc{x}+2|+C } \]

example.title: Integrating Quotients Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution

question.explanation:
Let $u=1+\tan^3x.$ Differentiating, we have \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 3\tan^2 x\cdot\sec^2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac13\textrm{d}u = \tan^2 x\sec^2x \,\textrm{d}x. \]

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \[ \eqalign{ \int \dfrac{\tan^2 x\sec^2x}{1+\tan^3x}\, \textrm{d}x &= \int \dfrac{1}{1+\tan^3x}\cdot\tan^2 x\sec^2x\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \int \dfrac{1}{u}\cdot\left(\dfrac13\textrm d u\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac13\int\dfrac{1}{u}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= \dfrac13\ln|u|+C\\[5pt] &= \dfrac13\ln|1+\tan^3x|+C\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\ln|1+\tan^3x|}{3} + C } \]

example.title: Integrating Quotients Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution

question.explanation:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because \[ \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(\cos^3{x}+1) =-3\cos^2{x} \sin{x}. \]

So, let $u=\cos^3{x}+1.$ Differentiating, we have

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=-3\cos^2{x} \sin{x}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\dfrac13\textrm{d}u=\cos^2{x} \sin{x} \, \textrm{d}x. \]

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

$x$ $0$ $\pi/3$
$u$ $2$ $9/8$

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

\begin{align*} \int_{0}^{\pi/3} \dfrac{\sin {x}\cos^2{x}}{\cos^3{x}+1}\,{\textrm{d}x} &= \int_{0}^{\pi/3}\dfrac{1}{\cos^3{x}+1}\cdot \sin {x}\cos^2{x}\, {\textrm{d}x}\\[5pt] &=\int_{2}^{9/8} \dfrac{1}{u}\cdot\left(-\dfrac13\right)\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac13\int_{2}^{9/8} \dfrac{1}{u}\,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac13\Big.\ln| u| \Big|_{2}^{9/8} \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac13\left(\ln \left(\dfrac98\right) - \ln \left(2\right)\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac13\left(\ln \left(2\right) - \ln \left(\dfrac98\right)\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac13\ln \left(\dfrac{2}{\left(\dfrac98\right)}\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac13\ln \left(\dfrac{16}{9}\right) \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
If we let $u = 2+\sec (x),$ then \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \sec (x) \tan (x) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}u = \sec( x) \tan (x) \,\textrm{d}x. \]

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

$x$ $0$ $\pi/3$
$u$ $3$ $4$

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \begin{align*} \int_{0}^{\pi/3}\dfrac{\sec( x) \tan (x)}{2+\sec (x)}\,{\textrm{d}x} &= \int_{0}^{\pi/3}\dfrac{1}{2+\sec (x)}\cdot \sec( x) \tan (x) \,{\textrm{d}x} \\[5pt] &= \int_{3}^{4} \dfrac{1}{u}\,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \ln|u| \,\Big|_{3}^{4} \\[5pt] &= \ln 4-\ln 3 \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\ln\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)} \end{align*}
